Physical binding approaches, ranked by how much they fight the fold.

**Coptic** — lies flat, exposed spine, the fold does the work.
**Case** — hides everything, will not lie flat.
**Japanese stab** — ignores the fold entirely, and is honest about it.

The ranking is really *how much does it fight the fold* — see
[[Quire Structures]] for why that is the axis that matters.

## Shortlist for the Bindery run

![[attachments/endpaper-01.svg]]
Indigo and gilt — the harbour-chart palette, reused
> Works because the gilt is a hairline, not a field. Any wider and it
> competes with the marbling instead of edging it.
> Reach for it when a dark cover needs a warm interior. See [[Quire Structures]].
#marbled #indigo

![[attachments/endpaper-02.svg]]
Walnut ink over cream. Warmest of the set
> The rule here is one pigment, two dilutions — the variation is water,
> not a second colour.
#marbled #warm

![[attachments/endpaper-03.svg]]
Sage and bone. Too quiet for a cover, right for endpapers
> Quiet is the point: an endpaper is read for two seconds while the book
> opens. Use where the cover is already loud.
#printed #green

## Rejected, kept for the colour

![[attachments/endpaper-04.svg]]
Aubergine. The one the client will not pick
> Kept for the colour relationship, not the sheet. The purple-to-rust
> jump is the useful part — see the Rust below.
#marbled #purple

![[attachments/endpaper-05.svg]]
Slate blue, almost grey. Safe choice
#printed #cool

![[attachments/endpaper-06.svg]]
Rust. Reads as older than it is
#marbled #warm

---

Gathering is the step where a stack of flat sheets becomes an object with a
spine, and it is the first point at which a mistake becomes expensive.

Four sheets folded together is a quire. Eight is comfortable. Sixteen is
showing off and will not lie flat for a decade.

See [[Quire Structures]]. Subjects: [[bookbinding]]

id: 01KVT5M0G0N07ZQ8ZAJ41Q7Q8X
kind: note
title: Lantern Cartography Notes
created: 2026-07-04T09:20:00+00:00
updated: 2026-08-26T09:20:00+00:00
tags: [current]
aliases: [Lantern Cartography Notes]
---

Field notes from three weeks of drawing harbour charts by lamp, which turns
out to be a legible constraint rather than an affectation.

A lantern gives you roughly a 300mm working circle. Everything outside it is
inferred. That is a limit on how much of a chart you can hold in your head at
once, and it shows up in the drawing: the older harbour charts have a dense,
confident centre and a vague, apologetic edge.

Modern tools removed the lamp and kept the habit. A canvas that scrolls forever
still produces work that is dense in the middle and vague at the edges — we just
stopped having a reason for it.

Related: [[Quire Structures]] on how the same limit shows up in binding.

Subjects: [[cartography]], [[typography]]

title: Quire Structures

updated: 2026-08-28T09:20:00+00:00
tags: [current]
aliases: [Quire Structures, Quires]
---

The running hub for how gathered sheets behave — structurally, and as a
metaphor I keep reaching for when a screen layout will not settle.

The through-line across everything below: **the fold is the unit, not the
page.** Anything that treats the page as atomic ends up fighting the object.

Subjects: [[bookbinding]], [[cartography]]

## Attachments

### Sheet counts per signature (markdown)

Four folios to a quire is the comfortable maximum for 90gsm — past that the
outer fold has to travel too far and the fore-edge steps visibly.

- **three sheets** — no step worth trimming
- **four sheets** — about a millimetre, the usual compromise
- **six sheets** — three millimetres, and it wants a plough

### The fold as a layout unit (link)
Source: https://example.com/fold-as-unit

The paragraph about scroll having no fold is the one worth arguing with.

## Links

- [[Lantern Cartography Notes]] — the same working-circle limit, different craft
- [[Folio Gathering Notes]] — where it becomes expensive
- [[Binding Methods]] — physical approaches, ranked against the fold
- [[Bindery]] — the project this feeds

**me** 2026-07-22T10:04:00+00:00
Is the quire actually a good metaphor for layout, or am I forcing it?

**me** 2026-07-28T16:41:00+00:00
Forcing it for grids. Not forcing it for scroll: a scroll has no fold, which is
exactly why long pages feel structureless.

The running hub for how gathered sheets behave — structurally, and as a
metaphor I keep reaching for when a screen layout will not settle.

The through-line across everything below: **the fold is the unit, not the
page.** Anything that treats the page as atomic ends up fighting the object.

Subjects: [[bookbinding]], [[cartography]]

## Attachments

### Sheet counts per signature (markdown)

Four folios to a quire is the comfortable maximum for 90gsm — past that the
outer fold has to travel too far and the fore-edge steps visibly.

- **three sheets** — no step worth trimming
- **four sheets** — about a millimetre, the usual compromise
- **six sheets** — three millimetres, and it wants a plough

Source: https://example.com/fold-as-unit
